article.title: AI Agents Need Permission Boundaries, Not Just Better Prompts
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
When a language model only writes text, a bad answer may confuse a user. When an AI agent can call tools, the same mistake can have a larger consequence. The agent may send a message, change a record, create a purchase request, or retrieve sensitive data. This is why agent safety cannot depend only on writing a better prompt. The system also needs permission boundaries.

A permission boundary defines what an agent is allowed to do, with which resources, and under what conditions. The principle is similar to access control for human employees and software services. An agent that only needs to read a customer profile should not automatically receive permission to edit the profile. An agent that drafts an email may not need permission to send it without approval.

Least privilege is a useful starting point. Give the agent the minimum access needed for its current job. This reduces the damage that can occur if the model misunderstands an instruction, a tool returns unexpected information, or malicious content tries to influence the agent. Permissions can also be separated by task. A research agent might have broad read access but no write access, while an operations agent may update a narrow set of records.

High-impact actions deserve stronger controls. Sending money, deleting data, changing security settings, signing contracts, or communicating externally may require human approval. The approval should happen close to the action and show the reviewer what the agent plans to do. A vague confirmation such as 'Continue?' is less useful than a clear statement of the target, amount, recipient, or record being changed.

Logging is another layer. Organizations need to know which agent called which tool, which parameters it used, what result came back, and whether a human approved the action. Logs help with incident investigation, quality improvement, and accountability. They are especially important when several agents can delegate work to one another.

Permissions should also expire or be revocable. An agent may need temporary access for one workflow but not permanent access. If a project ends, a user leaves the company, or suspicious behavior appears, the organization should be able to remove the permission quickly. Long-lived credentials increase risk because forgotten access can remain active after its original purpose disappears.

Prompt engineering still matters. Clear instructions reduce ambiguity and help an agent choose appropriate actions. But prompts are behavioral guidance, not a hard security boundary. A robust design assumes that a model can sometimes make a mistake and limits what that mistake can affect.

The practical question is therefore not only, 'Can the agent perform this task?' It is also, 'What is the smallest set of actions it should be allowed to perform?' Teams that answer both questions can build agents that are useful without giving every workflow unnecessary power.
paragraphs.zh: 當模型只能產生文字時，錯誤可能只是誤導；當 Agent 能呼叫工具時，錯誤可能直接改資料、發訊息或取得敏感資訊。因此安全不能只靠 prompt，而需要 permission boundary。核心做法是 least privilege：只給完成當前任務所需的最小權限。高影響動作如付款、刪資料、改安全設定或對外溝通可要求人工批准，而且批准畫面應清楚顯示即將執行的對象與內容。系統也應記錄 agent、tool、參數、結果與批准者，並讓權限可到期與撤銷。Prompt 是行為指引，不是硬性的 security boundary；設計上應假設模型有時會犯錯，再限制錯誤能造成的影響範圍。

phrases.example: Use least privilege for every agent.
A prompt is not a hard security boundary.

business.term: What is the minimum permission required?
business.example: What is the minimum permission required for this workflow?

quiz.question: Why are prompts not enough for agent security?
quiz.answer: Because prompts guide behavior but do not technically prevent unauthorized actions.

quiz.question: Output: Name one action that should require approval.
